title: Sex Education

jokes.text: Tom's defense: 'How dare you, sir? I was tweeting.'
jokes.setup: The judge asks Tom if he was texting at the time of his crash, implying reckless distraction.
jokes.punchline: Tom takes moral offense at 'texting' and corrects it to 'tweeting' — a distinction that makes him MORE guilty but which he treats as a point of pride.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy. The joke hinges on Tom's absurd social-media vanity: being called a 'texter' is a slight to his brand, even though both are equally dangerous. The indignation ('How dare you') immediately flips to self-incrimination. It is 100% character-specific — only Tom Haverford would care about this distinction in front of a judge. Earns a high score because it is simultaneously character comedy, ironic self-own, and a sharp satirical observation about social media obsession. Justifiably in the 8+ range.

dialogue.speaker: Judge
dialogue.line: Were you texting while driving?

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Texting? No, your honor, I was tweeting. There's a difference.

jokes.text: Tom's tweets read aloud in court: '9:17. Drive faster, blue Civic. Daaaaaamn. #soccermoms'
jokes.setup: The prosecutor reads Tom's Twitter feed leading up to the crash as Exhibit C.
jokes.punchline: The tweets reveal Tom's stream-of-consciousness social-media brain in real time, starting with mundane observations escalating toward disaster.
jokes.explanation: The tweet series works as an escalating joke machine, each tweet funnier than the last. '#soccermoms' is a great character-specific detail — Tom's brand-consciousness bleeding into road rage. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Judge
dialogue.line: What is this hashtag '#YoloSwag420'?

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Your Honor, that tweet was sent while I was driving to the courthouse. I was multitasking.

dialogue.speaker: Judge
dialogue.line: You were tweeting while operating a vehicle?

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: With all due respect, sir, the hashtag game waits for no man. And neither does traffic on I-96.

jokes.text: Tom's tweet mid-crash: 'Gotta pass this lady on the ejkerkj' — the tweet cuts off as he hits a fire hydrant.
jokes.setup: The prosecutor reads the sequence of tweets documenting Tom's distracted driving.
jokes.punchline: The final pre-crash tweet ends in gibberish ('ejkerkj') as Tom clearly lost control mid-tweet — then the next tweet confirms the crash.
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: the garbled text is the joke AND the evidence simultaneously. No extra words needed. The audience understands exactly what happened from the keyboard smash alone. It's visual comedy through text — a rare trick. Justifies 8+ for pure structural efficiency and originality of execution.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: The gibberish at the end of the tweet marks the exact moment of impact

jokes.text: Tom's post-crash tweet: '9:20. Just hit a fire hydrant, but I survived. #unbreakable. #what'sMr.Glassuptothesedays? ♪whynosequel?'
jokes.setup: Tom has just crashed into a fire hydrant while tweeting.
jokes.punchline: Rather than stopping, Tom immediately tweets about it with movie reference hashtags and a musical lament about there being no Unbreakable sequel — all while presumably still at the scene.
jokes.explanation: The Unbreakable reference is pitch-perfect Tom Haverford: pop-culture-fluent, self-dramatizing, and completely unconcerned with the actual emergency. The '♪ why no sequel?' sung hashtag is bizarre and delightful. High quotability because it's a specific enough cultural reference delivered in a unique format.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Okay, but to be clear, I did not hit that fire hydrant. That fire hydrant was already broken when I got there.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: In fact, I would argue that I actually helped it by giving it a little tap with my car.

jokes.text: Tom begs the bailiff: 'Pr-press send, bailiff! Press send!'
jokes.setup: The judge orders Tom to hand over his phone. Tom asks for 'one last tweet.'
jokes.punchline: The bailiff takes the phone before Tom can send it, and Tom desperately pleads with the bailiff to press send on his behalf.
jokes.explanation: A strong button on the cold open. Tom's addiction is so acute he's trying to deputize a court officer into sending his tweet. The desperation escalates the joke perfectly from the 'one last tweet' ask.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: #SurvivalInstinct #LuckyToBeAlive #BlessedAndGrateful #JustLikeInTheGreatOutdoorsPartII #ExceptWithoutDanAykroyd #AndWithMorePersonalInjuries

jokes.text: Leslie: 'A cowboy hat from your cowboyfriend.' Then correcting herself badly: 'From your cowboy boyfriend. Your boycow-cowboy.'
jokes.setup: Ann returns from a dude ranch wearing a cowboy hat given to her by her boyfriend Ricky.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately tries to make a portmanteau pun ('cowboyfriend'), is called out that it implies he's a cow, and then fumbles the correction so badly it becomes worse.
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining correction ('Your boycow-cowboy') is the best part — Leslie's inability to abandon a bad joke even when it fails is very in-character. The initial pun is groan-worthy in a fun way.

dialogue.speaker: Judge
dialogue.line: You are sentenced to one week without any screens or digital devices.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Your Honor, with all due respect, I would literally prefer actual incarceration.

jokes.text: Leslie announces with enthusiasm: 'Great news: Lots of old people have chlamydia.'
jokes.setup: Leslie calls a staff meeting, building up to 'great news.'
jokes.punchline: The 'great news' is that seniors have chlamydia — which is only great news from the perspective of a public health crusader who now has a mission.
jokes.explanation: Six words perfectly encapsulate Leslie Knope's character: her genuine enthusiasm for civic problems, her inability to read the room, and her framing of a public health crisis as an exciting opportunity. The joke is fully earned because it is 100% character-specific — no other character on television would say this with a straight face. High quotability. Justifies 8+ for economy and character integration alone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: No, no, no! Just let me finish this tweet! I'm in the middle of a thread! One more second!

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: You don't understand—this is important! My followers need to know about my lunch!

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Stop pulling me! I haven't even added the hashtags yet!

jokes.text: Leslie: 'What they're doing with that time is going at it hard, old people-style.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is briefing the team on the senior STD crisis.
jokes.punchline: The clinical phrase 'going at it hard, old people-style' is simultaneously specific and absurd — a government official's attempt to describe senior sex without euphemism.
jokes.explanation: Solid character-voice joke. The specificity of 'old people-style' does the heavy lifting. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: That makes him sound bovine.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'It's amazing what a few old guys can do with a little bit of charm and a lot of crabs.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is building her pitch for the sex education initiative.
jokes.punchline: The sentence begins like a feel-good story about charming seniors and ends with 'a lot of crabs' — a sudden pivot to an STD reference delivered with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed misdirection. The setup sounds like a compliment and 'crabs' lands hard as a punchline. Leslie's obliviousness to the absurdity she's producing elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Okay, so 'treat yo self' is good, but what if we did 'treat yourself'? No, that's just the full thing. What about 'treat yoself'? Still not working. Okay, 'treayoself'? 'Treatyoself'? 'Tre-yo-self'? I'm just saying random things now.

jokes.text: Leslie calls the team 'sex avengers' and refers to the seniors as 'hopped up on E.D. medication' with 'nothing to lose, 'cause they're close to death.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is rallying her team for the sex education mission.
jokes.punchline: The superhero framing ('sex avengers') combined with the blunt 'close to death' rationale for seniors' sexual recklessness is both dark and absurdly bureaucratic.
jokes.explanation: 'Sex avengers' is a great coinage and 'close to death' is a darkly funny rationale. The sequence is a little sprawling but each piece lands.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I have great news.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: We have an STD epidemic among seniors in Pawnee.

jokes.text: Tom/Andy role-playing as an old man: 'Actually, I think it's pronounced horny' — correcting Leslie's use of 'ornery.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says seniors can be 'pretty ornery.'
jokes.punchline: A character 'helpfully' corrects 'ornery' to 'horny' — pretending it's a mispronunciation while actually making a crude joke.
jokes.explanation: Simple wordplay that works in context. The correction format (pretending it's a genuine linguistic error) gives it a slightly elevated structure. Probably Andy given the naivety of the delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I have crabs.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Calm down. I bought them at the seafood market. They're in my office.

jokes.text: Old-person roleplay: 'I'm an old lady, why do I need birth control? I haven't had my monthly since LBJ was president.'
jokes.setup: The team pretends to be old people asking Ann sex questions to prep her for the seniors.
jokes.punchline: The birth control question is grounded in a delightfully specific historical reference (LBJ) that signals both age and the absurdity of the scenario.
jokes.explanation: The LBJ specificity is the joke — it's not just 'old lady' but a precisely calibrated historical timestamp. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: When you're that close to death, you stop caring about the rules. You're like, 'What are they gonna do, kill me? I'm already dying!'

jokes.text: Old-person roleplay escalation: 'Do pubic hairs get longer the older you get? Because that's happening to me. What should I do?'
jokes.setup: The roleplay continues with increasingly inappropriate questions.
jokes.punchline: The question shifts from general inquiry to an urgent personal confession — the character is not asking hypothetically.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from hypothetical to personal ('that's happening to me') is the joke's engine. Functional gross-out comedy, not particularly original but well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Seniors can be ornery.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Horny? I mean, I guess that's... that's great for them.

jokes.text: 'Where can I get lube that is healthy to eat?' followed by 'I ran over my testicles with my jazzy scooter.'
jokes.setup: The fake sex questions keep escalating in absurdity.
jokes.punchline: The lube-eating question is absurd enough, but the jazzy scooter testicle injury is a perfect image — specific, visual, and completely unexpected.
jokes.explanation: The jazzy scooter is the perfect prop for this joke — it's the mobility device most associated with elderly Americans, and the specificity of the injury ('ran over my testicles with my jazzy scooter') creates a vivid, ridiculous image. Strong escalation from the lube question.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: When did menopause start? Was it during the Bronze Age or the Iron Age?

jokes.text: 'I want to jump on that caboose. Choo choo!' directed at Ann during the roleplay.
jokes.setup: The old-person sex question roleplay is spiraling.
jokes.punchline: Someone abandons the pretense of asking a 'question' and just directly propositions Ann in character as an old man.
jokes.explanation: The train metaphor as a come-on is silly and the 'choo choo' sells it. Gets a laugh for pure absurdist commitment.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: I haven't felt this good since my last colonoscopy. The doctor said I had the colon of a 25-year-old. I'm not sure what that means, but I've been riding that high ever since.

jokes.text: Ann's triple response: 'You should never eat lube, you need to see a doctor immediately, and I'm sorry, sir, but you have to be under 40 to ride this train.'
jokes.setup: Ann has been barraged with absurd sex questions and a proposition.
jokes.punchline: Ann answers all three simultaneously in order, then plays along with the train metaphor to shut down the last questioner — a perfectly timed, clinically delivered triple punchline.
jokes.explanation: Structurally excellent. The joke requires the audience to remember all three preceding questions and then rewards them with perfectly ordered, economical responses. Ann using the train metaphor to reject the old man proposition ('under 40 to ride this train') is the best part — she's playing along while rejecting. A callback joke that works because the construction is impeccable. Justifies 7.8+ craft.

jokes.text: Tom calls his friend 'LeRon James' and arrives an hour and a half late because he couldn't use his GPS.
jokes.setup: Tom is screen-free for a week and had to navigate to work without GPS.
jokes.punchline: He 'figured it out' by driving in circles until he saw something familiar — and he lives 3 miles away.
jokes.explanation: 'LeRon James' as a person's name is a nice background gag. The navigation story is a solid illustration of Tom's complete tech dependency — 3.4 miles and he's helpless.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: I'm 87 years old. My back goes out more than I do.

jokes.text: Tom reveals his 'real-life Pinterest board' — a physical corkboard with items pinned to it.
jokes.setup: Tom is adapting to life without screens.
jokes.punchline: His solution to losing Pinterest is to recreate it physically — a literal corkboard — then laments: 'I really wish you could click those.'
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever visual joke that requires no explanation — the absurdity of recreating a digital interface physically is immediately funny. But 'I really wish you could click those' is the stroke of genius that elevates it: Tom understands the board is non-functional by digital standards but can't fully let go. Perfect character comedy. Justifies 8.0 craft — comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Why did the conductor keep looking back at the passenger car? Because he wanted to see if anyone was getting on... or off. Choo choo!

jokes.text: Tom explains his GPS-free navigation: 'I just drove around in circles until I saw something familiar.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been banned from screens and had to navigate to work without GPS.
jokes.punchline: His adaptation strategy is to drive in circles until something looks familiar — an absurd, inefficient, and completely Tom solution.
jokes.explanation: Efficiently funny and very Tom. He's so tech-dependent that basic pre-GPS navigation is genuinely beyond him. The circles strategy implies he has no spatial reasoning whatsoever. Good economy, strong character fit.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: I was at the station and saw a train... if you know what I mean.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Oh, you mean an actual train? Because the station does have excellent service during rush hour. They've really improved the scheduling.

jokes.text: April introduces herself to Congressman Murray as 'April Blart, mall cop.'
jokes.setup: Ben introduces himself professionally to their boss, Congressman Murray.
jokes.punchline: April gives a fake name combining her first name with 'Paul Blart: Mall Cop' — a deadpan non-sequitur that only April would do.
jokes.explanation: Pure April Ludgate: she does exactly what you'd least want an employee to do in a professional introduction. The Paul Blart reference is specific enough to be funny and stupid enough to be perfectly April. High character integration — no other character could deliver this.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Yo, LeRon James! What's good?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: It's Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I know what I said.

jokes.text: Ben's meeting prep with congressman is interrupted by the congressman's cheerful non-sequitur: 'Stay cool. It's a hot one out there today.'
jokes.setup: Ben is clearly trying to brief the Congressman on something substantive.
jokes.punchline: The Congressman responds with empty pleasantry — establishing him as politically hollow from his first moment.
jokes.explanation: Seeds the Congressman's running gag of empty platitudes. Gets funnier in retrospect as a setup for later payoffs.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I didn't use GPS. I just followed a guy who looked like he knew where he was going. Turned out he was lost too. We ended up at a Arby's in a strip mall. It took us forty-five minutes to go three miles.

jokes.text: Ben responding to April's 'Hey, we're still gonna assassinate him, right?' with 'Don't say that.'
jokes.setup: The team is prepping for a strategy session with a congressman.
jokes.punchline: April casually asks if assassination is still on the agenda in the same tone one would ask about a lunch order.
jokes.explanation: April's sociopathic casualness is the joke — the word 'assassinate' in a workplace comedy context, delivered as a procedural question. Ben's minimal horrified response is perfect straight-man work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I'm adapting to life without screens. I've created a physical recreation of my favorite digital platform.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I call it 'Pawnee-Face.' It's just me standing in the town square with a sign that says what I'm thinking, and people walk by and ignore me.

jokes.text: Talking head: What the hell is he doing? Cut to Congressman Murray staring blankly at nothing in his office.
jokes.setup: Ben and April are watching the congressman through glass.
jokes.punchline: The congressman is just... sitting. Staring. Doing absolutely nothing. Which Ben defends as 'thinking.'
jokes.explanation: The visual of a congressman in a nice office just sitting vacantly is the joke, and it sets up the robot running gag beautifully. Strong setup for later payoffs.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I want to pin this to my board, but also have it sync to the cloud.

jokes.text: Leslie's sex ed presentation to seniors: 'Does anyone know what we risk when we have unprotected sex?' — Answers include 'Heart attack,' 'Falling in love,' and 'Partner dies on top of you!'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks a standard sex-ed question to the audience of seniors.
jokes.punchline: The seniors' answers are an escalating mix of the medically plausible ('heart attack'), the romantically absurd ('falling in love'), and the darkly specific ('partner dies on top of you').
jokes.explanation: The escalation across three audience responses is well-paced. 'Partner dies on top of you' is the standout — specific, dark, and absolutely something an elderly person would know from experience. Gets a genuine surprise laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: April, that's not Obama.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: That congressman is white.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that's embarrassing.

jokes.text: Side character (Chris?) to Ben: 'Are these old people really having sex with each other?' / 'Yeah, what'd you think they were doing?' / 'I don't know, I thought we were just talking about it.'
jokes.setup: Two characters observe Leslie's sex ed seminar for seniors.
jokes.punchline: One character genuinely believed the sex ed class was purely theoretical for people who were no longer having sex.
jokes.explanation: A clean observational beat that gets a nice laugh from the absurdity of the assumption. Light but functional.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Paul Blart.

jokes.text: Senior audience member asks: 'What if the banana is soft and mushy, and doglegs sharply to the left?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is doing a condom demonstration using a banana, asking for audience participation.
jokes.punchline: A senior asks a question about the banana that is clearly about his own anatomy with the specificity that only someone speaking from experience would have.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'doglegs sharply to the left' is the punch. It's anatomically specific, delivered through the banana metaphor, and 'doglegs' is exactly the kind of term an older man would use. Economy is excellent — the metaphor does all the work. Strong impact.

dialogue.speaker: Congressman
dialogue.line: It's pretty hot out there.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: It really is. It's very hot. The heat is... it's a lot. Extremely hot. I would say it's one of the hottest days I can remember. Very, very hot.

jokes.text: Jerry navigating the internet: He goes to Altavista and types 'Please go to yahoo.com'
jokes.setup: Tom, bored without his phone, watches Jerry use a computer.
jokes.punchline: Jerry's internet navigation technique is to go to an ancient search engine and politely type a full sentence request to redirect to another site — treating the internet like a telephone operator.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely original joke about digital illiteracy. Altavista (an ancient search engine) is a specific, accurate detail that shows real writing craft. Jerry's use of 'Please' when addressing a search engine is the crowning detail — it's such a specific, human, wrong behavior. High character integration for Jerry (eternally hapless) and Tom (cannot contain his horror). Justifies 7.9 craft.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: So what's the strategy for the meeting?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: We're going to present the budget proposal and address their concerns about the timeline.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Have you considered just assassinating them?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: No, April, we've talked about this.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: It would solve a lot of problems.

jokes.text: Tom: 'You don't have your email bookmarked?' / Jerry: 'What's bookmarks?'
jokes.setup: Tom discovers Jerry doesn't have his email bookmarked.
jokes.punchline: Jerry doesn't know what bookmarks are — escalating his computer incompetence to a new level.
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation button on the previous joke. 'What's bookmarks?' is so simple it's devastating. The Altavista revelation made us think we'd reached the floor; this drops the floor again.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: He's just sitting there. Staring at nothing.

jokes.text: Tom: 'God, Jerry! You don't deserve the Internet!'
jokes.setup: Jerry reveals he doesn't know what bookmarks are.
jokes.punchline: Tom's existential verdict on Jerry's internet worthiness — delivered as a moral judgment rather than a technical critique.
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable line. Framing internet access as something to be DESERVED based on one's competence is a genuinely funny concept delivered with perfect economy. Strong Tom voice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: So, um, how often would you say you're sexually active?

dialogue.speaker: Elderly Woman
dialogue.line: Oh, I'd say three or four times a week. My husband and I, we'll have a threesome.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I'm going crazy, Ron! Life without screens is pointless. I made an iPhone out of paper. It's not the same, though.'
jokes.setup: Tom is at Ron's cabin, desperate without his devices.
jokes.punchline: Tom has crafted a paper iPhone — presumably with drawn-on icons — and laments that it lacks functionality. The visual of Tom holding a paper iPhone is the joke, confirmed by his sad addendum.
jokes.explanation: Echoes the Pinterest board joke with the same logic: Tom's coping mechanism for tech withdrawal is to recreate the physical objects. 'It's not the same, though' is a devastatingly obvious truth delivered with pathos.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What are some of the risks of unprotected sex?

dialogue.speaker: Senior #1
dialogue.line: Well, there's STDs.

dialogue.speaker: Senior #2
dialogue.line: Pregnancy.

dialogue.speaker: Senior #3
dialogue.line: Emotional trauma.

dialogue.speaker: Senior #4
dialogue.line: Your parents finding out.

dialogue.speaker: Senior #5
dialogue.line: A baby that resents you.

dialogue.speaker: Senior #1
dialogue.line: A lifetime of regret and loneliness.

dialogue.speaker: Senior #2
dialogue.line: Death.

jokes.text: Ron: 'We'll go to my cabin in the woods. It's so far away from civilization, the electric company is not even aware there's a structure there.'
jokes.setup: Ron prescribes a detox for Tom's screen addiction.
jokes.punchline: Ron's cabin is so off-grid that the utility company doesn't even know it exists — delivered as a perfectly matter-of-fact statement of pride.
jokes.explanation: Peak Ron Swanson characterization. The electric company not knowing the structure exists is the perfect quantifier of his off-grid philosophy — specific, plausible for Ron, and delivered with complete deadpan pride. High character integration: this line could only be Ron's.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: I assumed they would just teach it in theory.

jokes.text: Talking-head confessional describing Marshall Langman: 'Marcia is motivated, calculating, and hyper-vigilant, and her husband, Marshall, is... vivacious.'
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces the Langmans as the town's morality watchdogs.
jokes.punchline: 'Vivacious' — the long pause and wildly incongruous descriptor for an abstinence-crusading man implies a flamboyant quality that the show has clearly established visually.
jokes.explanation: The beat (the pause before 'vivacious') is where this joke lives. The contrast structure — three specific negative attributes for Marcia, then a searching pause and 'vivacious' for Marshall — is perfectly constructed. The word choice is key: 'vivacious' implies something about Marshall's presentation that the audience reads immediately. Economy is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Elderly Man
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, mine's more like a plantain at this point. Little darker, a little softer, and it smells like it's been sitting in a bowl for three weeks.

jokes.text: Marcia: 'If we allow this filth to be taught to our seniors, the next thing you know, it'll be in our high schools, then our kindergartens, and before you know it, we have babies in thong underwear.'
jokes.setup: Marcia is making a slippery-slope argument against senior sex education.
jokes.punchline: The slippery slope ends at 'babies in thong underwear' — an absurd terminus that the show refuses to explain or justify.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed slippery slope joke where the absurdity escalates perfectly and lands on a specific, ridiculous image. The logical chain is internally consistent in Marcia's worldview, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Jerry, your internet usage is a crime against humanity. You're streaming cat videos in 480p? That's not just bad, that's a personal attack on everyone with functioning eyeballs.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Tom, it's just the internet—

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Just the internet? JUST THE INTERNET? Jerry, you're literally the only person in this office who doesn't deserve high-speed connectivity. You should have to use dial-up. In 2015. As punishment.

jokes.text: Leslie's response to 'Is that what you want?' — 'Yes, that's what I want.'
jokes.setup: Marcia asks the rhetorical question 'Is that what you want?' about babies in thong underwear.
jokes.punchline: Leslie answers the rhetorical question literally and affirmatively, refusing to cede the rhetorical ground.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two words that do maximum work by treating a rhetorical question as literal. It's both a genuine expression of Leslie's stubbornness and a comedic move that wrongfoots Marcia.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I'm doing a physical recreation of my phone. Look, I'm swiping. Nothing's happening. That's the joke.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Andy, pack up our bananas!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is making a defiant exit from the senior center after being shut down.
jokes.punchline: Her rallying cry is about the condom-demonstration bananas — the absurdity of treating bananas as tactical equipment during a political retreat.
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfect economy, high quotability. The bananas as a symbol of her thwarted sex ed mission being packed up like weapons is a great button to the scene. Genuinely funny on reread.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Marshall is very... expressive. He's a free spirit. He marches to the beat of his own drum. He's not afraid to be himself, you know? He's colorful. He's vibrant. He's—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Look, Marshall is flamboyant, okay? The guy wears a ascot and drives a Prius with vanity plates.

jokes.text: Tom gets stung by a 'splinter' at Ron's cabin and immediately demands a phone with 4G to get on WebMD.
jokes.setup: Tom is at Ron's off-grid cabin, supposedly detoxing from screens.
jokes.punchline: A minor splinter sends Tom into full medical emergency mode — demanding a smartphone with 4G service, and specifically noting 'there's no time for the edge network.'
jokes.explanation: Tom's hypochondria-via-WebMD combined with his tech snobbery ('no time for the edge network') is a great character beat. The specificity of knowing the difference between 4G and edge while panicking about a splinter is very Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Marcia Langman
dialogue.line: If we teach kids about sex education, it's a slippery slope. Next thing you know, we'll have babies wearing thongs.

jokes.text: Ron instructs Tom to 'purge all this garbage' by talking about what he does on screens. Tom lists: 'Facebook, Twitter, Tumblr, Instagram... sometimes Linkedin, for the professional shorties.'
jokes.setup: Ron's detox therapy involves having Tom verbalize his internet habits so he can 'let them float away.'
jokes.punchline: 'For the professional shorties' — Tom's LinkedIn description reveals that even his professional networking is filtered through his style-over-substance persona. 'Shorties' in a LinkedIn context is absurd.
jokes.explanation: 'Professional shorties' is a great Tom Haverford phrase. The list itself (Facebook through LinkedIn) is observational, but the punchline qualifier makes it character-specific and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Marcia
dialogue.line: Who puts a baby in a thong?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: A baby who doesn't want tan lines.

jokes.text: Tom's new shirt conversation: 'It's not my favorite shirt, but it is my least favorite shirt.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks if Ben likes her new cowboy shirt from the dude ranch.
jokes.punchline: Ben's diplomatic non-compliment: it's not his 'least favorite' (a compliment) but also not his 'favorite' — creating a technically true but maximally unhelpful response.
jokes.explanation: Wait — re-reading: the line is 'It's not my favorite shirt, but it is my least favorite shirt.' This means it IS his least favorite — a politely phrased brutal insult. The politeness of the phrasing while delivering an absolute verdict is the joke. Good economy and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fine! I'm taking my bananas and going home!

jokes.text: Marcia on TV: 'We all have some crazy urges from time to time, but you just can't act on them. You have to bury them way down deep inside.'
jokes.setup: Marcia is on a local TV show advocating for abstinence.
jokes.punchline: Her description of 'burying urges way down deep inside' reads as an unconscious description of repression — especially given the 'vivacious' husband — and her delivery is intensely passionate.
jokes.explanation: Works as subtext comedy — the language of repression dressed up as virtue. Gets funnier in context of the vivacious husband reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have a splinter. A splinter! Do you know what the mortality rate is for splinters?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I need to look it up. Now. Where's my phone?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I can't remove it without knowing the exact removal procedure. What if I do it wrong? What if it gets infected?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I need WebMD. I need it right now.

jokes.text: Perd Hapley: 'There are some statistics that I'd like to share with you now, and they are numbers.'
jokes.setup: Perd is introducing statistics on his show.
jokes.punchline: Perd clarifies that the statistics are 'numbers' — his signature tautological, information-free journalism style.
jokes.explanation: Peak Perd Hapley. This is the platonic ideal of his character's joke — he promises information, then provides the most content-free possible clarification. 'Statistics... and they are numbers' is so precisely calibrated to his voice that it's almost a thesis statement for the character. High quotability. Justifies 8.3 for character integration and economy alone. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor for economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Ann's shirt is both a cowboy shirt and not a cowboy shirt at the same time. It's a Schrödinger's shirt. Until you observe it, it exists in a superposition of Western and non-Western states.

jokes.text: Marcia: 'And the other 15% are perverts. J.K., you guys.'
jokes.setup: Marcia cites that 85% of Pawnee supports abstinence-only education.
jokes.punchline: She calls the other 15% perverts, then 'jokes' ('J.K., you guys') — but the J.K. reads as totally insincere, revealing that she does actually think they're perverts.
jokes.explanation: The 'J.K.' (Just Kidding) on live television, delivered by a woman who clearly is NOT kidding, is a nice character beat. The text-speak 'J.K., you guys' from a morality crusader is also inherently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: Studies show that 60% of the time, abstinence works every time. I'm Perd Hapley.

jokes.text: Perd: '100% of Pawneeans are perd-verts. That's the name I call fans of this show based on the fact that my name is Perd.'
jokes.setup: Perd has been talking about abstinence statistics.
jokes.punchline: Perd invents a fan name for his show ('perd-verts') and then explains the etymology at length — as if the audience couldn't have figured out his name is 'Perd.'
jokes.explanation: Another Perd masterwork. The explanation of 'perd-verts' is unnecessary, condescending, and perfectly in character. That his fan name accidentally sounds like 'perverts' in a segment about abstinence is the episode's best structural irony. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chris Traeger
dialogue.line: Ann, I need you to stop the sex education class immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Why? What's wrong with it?

dialogue.speaker: Chris Traeger
dialogue.line: Well, I just got a complaint from a parent saying their child came home talking about 'playing with toys.' I will not have that kind of language in our schools.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Chris, they're educational toys. It's about demonstrating safe practices.

dialogue.speaker: Chris Traeger
dialogue.line: I don't care if they're made of solid gold. No playing with toys. Not on my watch.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Put away your sex toys and play with them on your own time.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is concluding a tense staff meeting about the abstinence-only law.
jokes.punchline: Leslie uses a sex-toy metaphor for metaphorical 'playing' — in a meeting about sex ed — with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Works because of the context — using a sex metaphor to dismiss people in a meeting about sex is inadvertently funny. Leslie's obliviousness is the engine.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: What is the congressman doing?

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Literally doing absolutely nothing all day.

jokes.text: Chris: 'I did eat all the bananas, so you can't play with those.'
jokes.setup: The team is discussing next steps after the bananas were used for a condom demonstration.
jokes.punchline: Chris has eaten the demonstration bananas, which is funny because (a) Chris's health food habits extend to eating prop food and (b) the bananas were for sex ed, which gives 'eating the bananas' an accidental innuendo.
jokes.explanation: The callback works — we were told to pack the bananas, so Chris eating them is a funny betrayal. Chris's health obsession consuming the sex-ed props is good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: You know he's not a robot, right?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Of course he's not a robot.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: His brain is just a computer going '01010101 consume babies consume babies consume babies.'

jokes.text: April's theory about the congressman: 'He's a robot.' Ben: 'He's not a robot.' April: 'Like, One, one, zero, one. Must eat babies for fuel.'
jokes.setup: Ben and April are watching the congressman stare blankly at nothing.
jokes.punchline: April's robot binary code theory extends to the congressman needing to eat babies for organic fuel — a bizarre escalation that mixes sci-fi logic with horror.
jokes.explanation: April's deadpan commitment to the robot theory is very in-character, and 'must eat babies for fuel' is a wonderfully dark escalation. Ben's follow-up logic check ('Why would a robot need to consume organic matter?') is a perfect straight-man response that makes the exchange funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Congressman
dialogue.line: Is there anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Beep boop beep boop.

jokes.text: April: 'He's a robot.' Ben: 'He's not a robot.' April: 'He's just thinking. He's got a lot on his mind.' Ben: 'Yeah, like one, one, zero, one. Must eat babies for fuel.'
jokes.setup: Ben and April are debating whether Congressman Murray is a robot based on his complete stillness.
jokes.punchline: Ben dismisses April's robot theory and then immediately does a robot impression including baby-eating — undercutting his own defense.
jokes.explanation: 'Must eat babies for fuel' is the comedic peak — specifically because it's so unnecessary and dark for someone defending the non-robot theory. Ben doing a robot voice while insisting there's no robot is the structural irony. Good absurdist riff.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I'm doing a technology detox. No phones, no computers, no tablets. I'm going back to basics.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: But I will say, Wikipedia is incredible. It's like having the entire world's knowledge at your fingertips. Every single article is perfect. There are no errors. It's basically the Bible, except it's real and it's better written.

jokes.text: Ben enters and tells the congressman he's brought a briefing packet. Congressman says 'Excellent, thank you.' / 'Anything else I can do for you?' / 'No sir. All systems are operational.'
jokes.setup: April has just theorized the congressman is a robot.
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately catches himself saying 'all systems are operational' to the congressman — language that confirms the robot suspicion — then awkwardly exits.
jokes.explanation: The payoff is beautifully constructed: April planted the robot theory, and now Ben is unconsciously fulfilling it by using robotic language. The rewatch bonus is high — on second viewing, knowing the payoff is coming makes the setup funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I chat with Brad Pitt all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: It's not the actor, just a random teacher I talk to regularly.

jokes.text: Tom's internet monologue continues: Wikipedia leads him from Ray J to his Snoop Dogg connection to Mars Attacks in under a paragraph. 'Suddenly, you're on the Mars Attacks page.'
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining all the things he misses about the internet to Ron.
jokes.punchline: Tom's description of a Wikipedia rabbit hole — starting at Ray J's sex tape and ending at Tim Burton's Mars Attacks — is a perfectly accurate recreation of how Wikipedia actually works.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the Wikipedia path (Ray J → Snoop Dogg cousin → Mars Attacks) is accurate enough to be recognizable and absurd enough to be funny. Tom's earnest love of this process is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Okay, so emoji are just little pictures, right? But here's the thing - they're racist. Look at this one. This is clearly a Asian businessman emoji. But this one? This is just a regular businessman emoji. So what you're telling me is that one ethnicity of businessman gets special treatment? That's discrimination. And another thing - why is there a taco emoji but no pizza emoji? Oh wait, there is a pizza emoji. Why is there a taco emoji AND a pizza emoji? Because apparently we need to acknowledge every food group, but we can't just have one generic businessman? This is political correctness gone mad.

jokes.text: Tom explains emoji: 'Instead of saying What up, boo?, you can type What up and then a cute little ghost, 'cause that means boo.' Then: 'There's even a little Indian guy, but he has a turban on, which I think is racist, but the Asian guy also has a racist hat on, and it's like, Hold up, didn't Japanese people invent this?'
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining emoji to Ron as part of his internet monologue.
jokes.punchline: Tom simultaneously explains emoji, uses one correctly (boo/ghost), and then launches a cultural critique of emoji representation that's both self-aware and absurd.
jokes.explanation: The ghost = boo explanation is a genuine insight delivered with Tom's particular brand of enthusiasm. The emoji representation critique ('didn't Japanese people invent this?') is unexpectedly sharp cultural commentary from Tom, which makes it funnier coming from him.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm starting a podcast. It's called 'Treat Yo' Shelf: A Podcast About Organizing Your Spice Rack Alphabetically.' First episode: 'Paprika: Am I Doing This Right?'

jokes.text: Tom: 'Jean-Ralphio and I have a podcast called Nacho Average Podcast where we rate different kinds of nachos.'
jokes.setup: Tom is listing all his internet activities for Ron.
jokes.punchline: Tom and Jean-Ralphio's podcast is the most on-brand possible content for both characters — nachos rated with the solemnity of a serious podcast.
jokes.explanation: The name 'Nacho Average Podcast' is Tom and Jean-Ralphio in a nutshell — the pun, the food, the narcissistic passion project. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: He's overwhelmed by the volume of Tom's digital life.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I had no idea how much you had in your system. This is a real problem, Tom. You are an addict.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been talking for what feels like forever about his internet habits.
jokes.punchline: Ron, who prescribed the 'talk it out' therapy, discovers it has produced the opposite of catharsis — and delivers his diagnosis with complete clinical gravity.
jokes.explanation: Ron's backfired therapeutic experiment is a good character beat. His reluctant admission that he 'had no idea' is very Ron — the man who prescribed the treatment being dismayed by its effect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I know how to handle Tom's addiction. I learned addiction treatment from downloading TV shows.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I've downloaded every episode of Intervention. I know what to do here.' Ron: 'I'm proud of you, but also a bit fearful that we're verging on what I call feelings territory, so let's stare at the fire in silence.'
jokes.setup: Tom has a breakthrough and accepts he's an addict. Ron is moved.
jokes.punchline: Ron shuts down any emotional connection by declaring they've reached 'feelings territory' and prescribing silent fire-staring instead.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Feelings territory' is a perfect Ron Swanson coinage — he has a name for this zone and he actively avoids it. The remedy ('stare at the fire in silence') is exactly what Ron would prescribe and exactly what would make Ron feel better. Tom downloading every episode of Intervention as his therapy research is also a great character beat. High character integration on both. Justifies 8.2 craft — the joke is constructed around both characters' essences simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Stopping all sex isn't going to happen.

dialogue.speaker: Marcia Langman
dialogue.line: Well, not with that attitude. You're going to give yourself away at the Bone Zone.

jokes.text: Tom's practiced 'addict' speech: 'I am an addict. I've hurt all my friends and family with my addiction. I will accept this gift of rehabilitation.'
jokes.setup: Ron has told Tom he's an addict and needs to change.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately deploys a perfectly rehearsed recovery speech — which means he's not actually processing this, he's performing recovery because he watched Intervention too.
jokes.explanation: The scripted quality of Tom's response is the joke — he's reciting recovery language without actually feeling it. Good callback to the Intervention setup. The phrase 'gift of rehabilitation' is the tell — too formal for genuine feeling.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: It's Transylvania, not Tramp-sylvania.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: And Marshall, I don't need your encouragement right now.

jokes.text: Tom's 'breakthrough': 'I've had a breakthrough, Ron. What do you say you chop up some more wood, and I'll take your car and go grab us some victory steaks?'
jokes.setup: Tom and Ron have shared a genuine bonding moment about Tom's addiction.
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'breakthrough' is immediately revealed as a manipulation to get Ron's car keys so he can presumably go buy a phone. The 'victory steaks' framing is a Tom Haverford-level spin.
jokes.explanation: The con is perfectly structured — Tom sets up Ron's emotions with the 'breakthrough' and then immediately tries to convert the goodwill into car keys. 'Victory steaks' is a great Tom detail: he's framing this as a celebratory tradition when it's actually an escape attempt.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, you're... you're the one who's changing personalities!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know that doesn't even make sense.

jokes.text: Marcia accuses Leslie of coming from 'Tramp-sylvania.' Leslie: 'I'm from Michigan!' Ben: 'That wasn't worth saying.'
jokes.setup: Marcia is insulting Leslie's sexual permissiveness.
jokes.punchline: Marcia's geographic slur ('Tramp-sylvania') is so weak that Ben — Leslie's ally — immediately editorializes that it 'wasn't worth saying.'
jokes.explanation: Ben's 'that wasn't worth saying' is the real joke — it's directed at Leslie's rebuttal ('I'm from Michigan'), which was itself so mundane that it warranted the dismissal. A two-beat joke where the punchline punctures both combatants.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ann, you can't change who you are for a guy. But if you want to wear that incredible pearl-snap Western shirt with the fringe, and those boots that make your calves look like a young Raquel Welch, then do that for you. Because you look like a sexy ranch owner who also does philanthropy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Thank you.

jokes.text: Leslie to Ann: 'When you dated Andy, you dressed in flannels. When you dated Chris, you dressed in spandex.'
jokes.setup: Leslie confronts Ann about losing herself in relationships, as Ann is currently dressed as a cowgirl for boyfriend Ricky.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's specific recall of Ann's past fashion phases for each boyfriend is both an accurate character observation and a gentle roasting — the flannel/spandex detail is specific enough to be funny.
jokes.explanation: For longtime viewers, the callback to Andy's flannel aesthetic and Chris's athletic phase is a satisfying character-continuity joke. Rewards loyal viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I was driving, and a squirrel ran in front of the car, so I swerved to avoid it. Then a raccoon came out of nowhere, so I swerved the other way. Then a deer jumped out, so I swerved again. Then a bear started chasing the car, so I just drove into a tree to be safe.

jokes.text: Ann: 'You're dressed like an abstinence girl on the outside!' Leslie: 'God, I'm off my comeback game right now.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is criticizing Ann's cowgirl outfit. Ann retorts that Leslie is dressed conservatively because she's been forced to advocate for abstinence.
jokes.punchline: Leslie acknowledges mid-argument that her comeback was weak — breaking the fourth wall of the argument to critique her own performance.
jokes.explanation: Leslie self-aware enough to know her comeback failed mid-battle is funny — she's competitive enough that losing a verbal exchange is its own kind of pain. The meta-commentary on her own performance is a good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo! It's T-Dawg in the house with my new smartphone. I'm basically a tech genius now.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, that's absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, you wouldn't understand. I'm about to go viral. That's what the kids call it, right? I'm going to be so viral.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Please stop talking.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My new name is Tom Haverfard, but you can call me T-Dawg Swag Master 3000. That's my handle.

jokes.text: Leslie to Ann: 'Girl, you look like Annie Oakley and Pippi Longstocking had a baby and I love it.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann have just had a sharp argument. Leslie tells Ann to do whatever she wants.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately pivots to complimenting Ann's ridiculous cowgirl outfit by comparing her to Annie Oakley and Pippi Longstocking — and genuinely loving it.
jokes.explanation: The Leslie-Ann friendship in a single line. The specific pairing of Annie Oakley and Pippi Longstocking is unexpectedly accurate and vivid, and the 'I love it' button — which is completely sincere — is the emotional pivot that makes it land. This is warm character comedy at its best. Justifies 8.0 craft: the specificity of the comparison, the emotional whiplash from the argument, and the pure warmth of Leslie's genuine admiration are all doing heavy lifting simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Marshall Langman
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo. My name is Marshall and I'm here to say, I practice abstinence in a major way. I don't have sex, it's not for me, I'd rather watch TV and drink my tea. Abstinence is the way, don't delay, wrap it up or look the other way!

jokes.text: Tom returns, driving through the woods despite having no screens: 'A deer jumped in front of the car, and then a bear jumped in front of the deer!'
jokes.setup: Ron gave Tom his car keys (to get victory steaks). Tom is back immediately.
jokes.punchline: Tom's alibi for his quick return is a wildlife escalation — deer, then bear — that sounds like Tom misremembered or invented it in the moment.
jokes.explanation: Functional joke that confirms Tom went to buy a phone. The deer/bear escalation is mildly amusing but doesn't land as hard as the surrounding material.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You should wait until marriage to have sex.

dialogue.speaker: Elderly Woman
dialogue.line: I'm 87 years old. If I wait until marriage, I'll be dead.

jokes.text: Perd on the news: 'The story of that commercial break is it's over.'
jokes.setup: Perd is returning from a commercial break.
jokes.punchline: Perd's transition from commercial break is to announce that the commercial break is over — stating only the self-evident fact of the moment.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Perd Hapley lines in the episode. 'The story of that commercial break is it's over' is a perfect encapsulation of his character: he uses a journalistic framing device ('the story of...') to communicate something completely content-free. It's pure Perd. Exceptional character integration and economy. Earns 8+ — one of the episode's standout jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Okay, so according to this abstinence pamphlet, if you have premarital sex, the devil will inhabit your body parts. Your mouth becomes the devil's puppet. Your hands become the devil's tools. And your genitals become the devil's... playground.

jokes.text: Tom has a new phone and tweets: 'Tommy-edamame is back on the grid. Tell everyone to light me up with their dijjies, gotta load 'em into my burner.'
jokes.setup: Tom snuck off to buy a phone while Ron was chopping wood.
jokes.punchline: Tom's first communication back on his new phone uses incomprehensible Tom-speak ('dijjies,' 'burner,' 'Tommy-edamame') that reveals how deeply his social media persona is its own language.
jokes.explanation: 'Tommy-edamame' is inspired — edamame as a nickname element is so random it could only be Tom. 'Dijjies' is pure made-up Tom jargon. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. You want abstinence education? Here it is: Don't have sex. Because you will get pregnant and die.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, not die. But you might get diabetes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Anyway, here's some contraception pamphlets, a list of local clinics, and my personal phone number if you have questions about safe sex practices.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Out of the car, now. Where are we going, Ron? Are we walking to best buy to get a better phone?'
jokes.setup: Ron discovers Tom bought a new phone instead of getting steaks.
jokes.punchline: Tom, mid-punishment, asks if they're walking to Best Buy so he can upgrade the phone he just bought — prioritizing the phone quality over the consequence.
jokes.explanation: Tom's absolute inability to process that he's in trouble because he's already thinking about phone upgrades is great character work. Shows addiction logic perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Chris Traeger
dialogue.line: As your supervisor, I have to advise you to follow proper protocol and document everything in triplicate.

dialogue.speaker: Chris Traeger
dialogue.line: But between you and me, that's bureaucratic nonsense. Just do what you think is right.

jokes.text: Marshall Langman's rap: '♪ I'm Marshall Langman and I'm here to say / that sex before marriage is never the way / I waited till marriage and then some to do it / if you decide to sin, you'll rue it! ♪ Word.'
jokes.setup: Marshall appears at the senior center to deliver an abstinence message.
jokes.punchline: Marshall delivers his abstinence message as a hip-hop rap, complete with 'Word' at the end — a middle-aged conservative man performing a genre associated with everything he opposes.
jokes.explanation: Marshall's rap is a perfect expression of the 'vivacious' characterization — the conservative anti-sex crusader who secretly is very much not the uptight man his wife is. 'I waited till marriage and then some to do it' is a fascinating line ('and then some' implies even beyond marriage he was abstaining?) and 'Word' as a button is perfect. High quotability and rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why does he move like a robot?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's ideal political behavior. You want to seem human enough that people don't realize you're a lizard person, but robotic enough that they don't expect you to have feelings or opinions.

jokes.text: Senior audience member: 'I am not going to be told not to have sex by someone who's ten years my junior.' — Other senior: 'Amen, Gladys. You're right!' / Leslie: 'Not about the age thing, about the other thing.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is delivering the mandated abstinence message to seniors.
jokes.punchline: A senior objects on generational grounds (age), not moral ones. Another senior agrees — but Leslie has to clarify they're agreeing about abstinence, not about the age hierarchy.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's clarification ('not about the age thing') is a well-timed beat — she has to actively manage which argument her audience is agreeing with. Good structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Why do you need constant digital distraction?

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Because reality is disappointing and my phone is amazing.

jokes.text: Pamphlet reading: 'The devil likes to hide in all your private nooks and crannies, and if you open too wide, he might get out, or in.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is forced to read from the abstinence pamphlet 'So You Think You Know More Than God.'
jokes.punchline: The pamphlet's theology is unintentionally sexual — 'private nooks and crannies,' 'open too wide,' 'get out, or in' — written by someone apparently unaware of how it sounds.
jokes.explanation: The inadvertent innuendo of the abstinence pamphlet is a classic comedy construction — language that intends purity reads as lewdness. 'Nooks and crannies,' 'open too wide,' and the ambiguous 'get out, or in' escalate perfectly. Leslie's 'What...?' reaction sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: I lost myself in that relationship. I was doing things I never thought I'd do.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: I bought a horse. A HORSE. I wore a bolo tie. I went to a gun show... voluntarily.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: I said 'y'all' unironically. Multiple times. In one sentence.

jokes.text: Senior: 'Can we just see the condom demonstration again? 'Cause I don't know where Lou has been.'
jokes.setup: The seniors are being subjected to the abstinence pamphlet reading.
jokes.punchline: A senior requests the practical safe sex demonstration, specifically citing that she doesn't know her partner Lou's sexual history — making the public health case with personal urgency.
jokes.explanation: 'I don't know where Lou has been' is a perfectly economical line that does everything — it establishes that Lou is a real person, implies a complicated romantic situation, and makes the public health argument more vividly than any statistic. High quotability. The specificity of the name 'Lou' is exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ann, you are such a beautiful heifer.

jokes.text: Leslie snaps and delivers an impromptu condom demonstration: 'Screw it. Okay, here. This is a penis, right? You put a condom on it...' then: 'Condoms for everybody! Who wants some?'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been forced to read from the abstinence pamphlet despite knowing it's wrong.
jokes.punchline: Leslie abandons restraint and delivers a frank condom demonstration to elderly strangers, capping it with 'Condoms for everybody! Who wants some?' like she's handing out free samples.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's breaking point is perfectly earned — the audience has watched her hold back for the whole episode, and her release ('Screw it') followed by 'Condoms for everybody!' is the emotional payoff. The 'Oprah giving out cars' energy of 'Who wants some?' is inspired. High character integration: this is Leslie doing what Leslie does — ignoring political risk to do what she believes is right, and doing it with maximum enthusiasm. Justifies near-8 craft.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: You break it, you buy it doesn't apply to censure. I learned that the hard way at Pier 1.

jokes.text: Chris: 'It's a censure from the mayor's office. It's so official. I mean, look at the paper quality. This is no joke.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been officially censured for her condom demonstration.
jokes.punchline: Chris is awed by the paper quality of the censure document — his hyper-positivity extending to admiring the production values of his friend's official reprimand.
jokes.explanation: Chris Traeger's compulsive positivity finding something to admire in a censure document is perfect character comedy. 'Look at the paper quality' is a funny specific detail for him to latch onto.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It's a book. Paper. Bound together. Words printed on the pages. You read them. With your eyes. One page at a time. No battery required. No notifications. No algorithm deciding what you read next. You decide. You control the pace. It's just you and the author having a conversation across time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Does it come in a smaller size? Like for my phone?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It IS the smaller size.

jokes.text: Leslie to Chris: 'Why am I still weirdly scared of you?' Chris: 'I'm very confident and I make a lot of eye contact.'
jokes.setup: Chris has just reminded Leslie that she's now his boss as a council member.
jokes.punchline: Leslie asks why she's still intimidated. Chris's self-aware answer — 'I'm very confident and I make a lot of eye contact' — is both genuinely true to his character and a funny self-analysis.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect two-line exchange. Chris's answer is simultaneously self-aware, accurate, and completely unselfconscious — he's not being arrogant, he's giving a genuine behavioural explanation for his intimidating presence. 'I make a lot of eye contact' as a source of social power is a precise and funny observation. Justifies 8.0 craft for economy and character integration. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My fellow Americans, I come before you today to discuss the critical issues facing our great nation.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh my God. He's been turned into a robot.

jokes.text: Chris to Leslie (in private): 'Between you and me, as your best friend... I kind of admire what you did up there.'
jokes.setup: Chris has officially recommended Leslie apologize and follow the law.
jokes.punchline: Chris immediately switches from city manager mode to best friend mode, confessing he secretly admired her rule-breaking — showing his dual loyalties with no apparent conflict.
jokes.explanation: Warm character beat that plays on Chris's earnestness. The 'Wha—?' reaction to the sudden mode switch suggests a physical comedy beat. Functional but not a strong joke structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: We should go eat. I have been programmed to enjoy consuming nutrients— I mean, I really enjoy eating.

jokes.text: Chris: '...but between you and me, as your best friend... (dramatic pause) I kind of admire what you did up there.'
jokes.setup: Chris is giving Leslie official advice to apologize for breaking the abstinence law.
jokes.punchline: Chris transitions from 'city manager' mode to 'best friend' mode mid-sentence — the 'best friend' designation is so formal and dramatic it's funny.
jokes.explanation: Chris officially declaring a mode switch to 'best friend' is a good character beat. His intense need to be everyone's best friend is a core trait. Mild but warm comedy.

jokes.text: Congressman Murray's stump speech: 'We've gone through some difficult times, but we're from Ohio. We're tough...' followed by 'Cool beans. See you guys later.'
jokes.setup: Ben has asked the congressman to run through his stump speech to test the satellite feed.
jokes.punchline: The congressman delivers a passable political speech and then immediately breaks character with 'Cool beans' — revealing the total vacuity beneath the polished performance.
jokes.explanation: The contrast between the stirring political speech and 'cool beans' is the joke. 'Cool beans' is perfectly chosen — it's the most generic, hollow sign-off imaginable, revealing the congressman as a human applause machine with only a few operating phrases in his repertoire.

jokes.text: Ben talking head: 'God, I love him. He's the best.' — delivered with complete sincerity about a man who just said 'cool beans.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just watched the congressman say 'Cool beans' and leave.
jokes.punchline: Ben's genuine, unironic enthusiasm for the congressman — despite having watched him do nothing of substance all episode — reveals Ben's professional servility.
jokes.explanation: The payoff for the congressman's running gag. Ben's absolute conviction that this man is great — after watching him do essentially nothing — is the joke. The irony is that Ben isn't being sarcastic; he genuinely means it, which is funnier.

jokes.text: Tom's confession: 'The truth is I spend a lot of time looking at screens because recently, a lot of the stuff in my real life isn't going that great. So I'd rather play Doodle Jump than think about that.'
jokes.setup: Ron asks why Tom needs constant distraction.
jokes.punchline: Tom's genuine, vulnerable confession about using Doodle Jump as escapism from his actual life problems is both touching and funny — the specificity of 'Doodle Jump' deflates any potential sentimentality.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode structurally because it's also the episode's emotional core. The specific choice of 'Doodle Jump' (a notably simple, repetitive game) as the thing Tom prefers to real life is perfectly calibrated — it's both funny and a little sad. The joke earns its emotional weight without being manipulative. Justifies 8.1 craft for the marriage of character insight and comedic economy.

jokes.text: Ron: 'And while you're there, neither doodle nor jump.'
jokes.setup: Ron tells Tom to sit in his office while he decides whether to report him to the judge.
jokes.punchline: Ron's deadpan instruction not to 'doodle or jump' — a literal, earnest prohibition parsed from the game name — is Ron applying his characteristic literal-mindedness to a joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Pure Ron Swanson. He takes the brand name 'Doodle Jump,' separates it into its component words, and issues them as individual prohibitions — treating it as a literal behavioral instruction rather than a game title. The construction is perfect: four words, maximum character specificity, maximum comedic economy. This is what 8+ looks like. Highly quotable. Justifies 8.3 craft.

jokes.text: Ann: 'I broke it off with Ricky.' Leslie: 'Well, that's good, but I'll tell you, he'll never lasso another heifer as fine as you, Annie Oakley.'
jokes.setup: Ann tells Leslie she broke up with Ricky and is working on being more herself.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's condolence is a 'compliment' that calls Ann a heifer — delivered with complete sincerity as the nicest possible thing to say.
jokes.explanation: Leslie calling Ann a heifer while meaning it as the highest possible compliment is both character-perfect and structurally funny. The cowboy motif makes 'heifer' the logical compliment in Leslie's mind — she's staying in the metaphor while accidentally insulting her best friend. 'Annie Oakley' callback is a nice button.

jokes.text: Ann: 'I turned all my jeans into Daisy Dukes.'
jokes.setup: Ann is listing the ways she lost herself in the cowboy relationship aesthetic.
jokes.punchline: 'All my jeans' — not some, all of them. She committed so fully to the Daisy Duke aesthetic that she has no non-shorts pants left.
jokes.explanation: 'All my jeans' is the load-bearing comic word — the totality of her commitment to a temporary aesthetic. Classic escalation of Ann's identity-absorption pattern.

jokes.text: Perd: 'Leslie, what exactly does censure mean?' Leslie: 'It means I have been formally disciplined for breaking the law.' Perd: 'Well, you know what they say, you break it, you buy it.' Leslie: 'That doesn't really apply here.' Perd: 'Tell that to the folks at Pier 1, an establishment I'm no longer allowed inside.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to make a public statement about her censure on Perd's show.
jokes.punchline: Perd misapplies the 'you break it, you buy it' idiom to a legal censure, then reveals he was banned from Pier 1 (a home goods store) through some unspecified incident.
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best jokes. Perd's misapplication of the idiom is funny enough, but 'Tell that to the folks at Pier 1, an establishment I'm no longer allowed inside' is the line of the episode outside the main character moments. The specificity of Pier 1 (a mildly twee home decor store), the formality of 'an establishment I'm no longer allowed inside,' and the complete absence of explanation for what happened — all delivered with Perd's signature oblivious authority — is pitch-perfect character comedy. Justifies 8.4 craft: original, structurally elegant, maximally character-integrated, and completely quotable.

jokes.text: Leslie pins the censure document to her blazer like a badge of honor. Perd: 'Wow, strong words from a woman who is trying to pin a piece of paper to her blazer.'
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers a rousing speech about wearing her censure 'proudly, like a badge of honor.'
jokes.punchline: The visual of Leslie literally trying to pin a piece of paper to her blazer mid-speech undercuts the rhetorical gravitas perfectly, and Perd observes it with his characteristic deadpan literalism.
jokes.explanation: The joke requires both the visual (Leslie fumbling with a piece of paper) and Perd's commentary to land. The structure is: Leslie's speech builds to a metaphor → she literalizes the metaphor → the literalization is physically awkward → Perd narrates the awkwardness. It's a four-step joke executed in one beat. Justifies 8.1 craft for structural elegance.

jokes.text: Perd announces his new segment: 'Are you there, perd-verts? It's me, Perd, hosting a new segment.'
jokes.setup: Perd is introducing a new viewer call-in segment.
jokes.punchline: The segment name is a Judy Blume reference ('Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret') with Perd substituting himself — but he then adds 'hosting a new segment' because the title doesn't include enough literal description.
jokes.explanation: The addition of 'hosting a new segment' after the literary reference title is classic Perd — he cannot let a phrase stand without annotating it with additional obvious information. The Judy Blume reference is a bonus for anyone who recognizes it. Good Perd character work.

jokes.text: Ron presents Tom with a paper book: 'I am giving you a non-electronic book made of paper from a tree. It is called Auto Repair Manual: 1982.'
jokes.setup: Tom hopes Ron is giving him his iPhone back.
jokes.punchline: Ron's description of a book ('non-electronic, made of paper from a tree') treats it as an exotic artifact, and the specific title — Auto Repair Manual: 1982 — is the least digital, least Tom thing imaginable.
jokes.explanation: Ron describing a book as 'non-electronic, made of paper from a tree' is perfect Ron — he's not being condescending, he's genuinely explaining what a book is from first principles for Tom's benefit. The 1982 Auto Repair Manual is the most Ron-specific gift imaginable: practical, analog, masculine, and completely useless to Tom. High character integration for both. Justifies 8.0 craft.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I'm so bored.' — sitting in the office without screens, staring at nothing.
jokes.setup: Ron has told Tom to sit in his office while he considers whether to report him to the judge.
jokes.punchline: Tom's existential announcement of boredom — with zero screens and nothing to do — is the simplest possible expression of his character's core dependency.
jokes.explanation: A functional button on the Tom-without-screens arc. The absolute minimalism ('I'm so bored') after a whole episode of elaborate adaptations is a mild laugh. Not a standout moment but consistent.

jokes.text: Ron: 'And second, if you ever need to discuss your problems with someone... find Leslie. She lives for that crap.'
jokes.setup: Ron is giving Tom life advice in his characteristic way, having avoided 'feelings territory' all episode.
jokes.punchline: Ron's advice for emotional support is to outsource it entirely to Leslie — and his description of Leslie's passion for emotional support as 'she lives for that crap' is simultaneously dismissive and accurate.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's warmest and funniest lines. Ron's advice IS affectionate — he's directing Tom to the right person — but his language ('she lives for that crap') maintains his emotional armor perfectly. It's a love letter to Leslie written in Ron's voice. High character integration for both Ron and Leslie. Justifies 8.0 craft for the simultaneous characterization of three people in one line.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'The Pawnee Sun is calling me Loose-ly Grope. But you know what? I don't even care. I'm gonna kick all their asses!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is energized by the controversy and the censure.
jokes.punchline: 'Loose-ly Grope' as the newspaper's nickname for Leslie is a juvenile pun that the show presents without endorsing, and Leslie's complete dismissal of it ('I don't even care') before going into full battle mode is very Leslie.
jokes.explanation: 'Loose-ly Grope' is a deliberately weak pun — it's supposed to be a small-town newspaper's best effort. Leslie's energy despite the insult is the character joke.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I'm gonna go right now and drink, like, 1,000 Red Bulls so I can draft a new bill to undo abstinence-only.' Ben: 'Man, you are just a machine.' Leslie: 'But you're gonna have to take out a lot of cursing, 'cause like I said, I am very fired up.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is energized and ready to fight.
jokes.punchline: Leslie pre-warns Ben that her draft will be full of cursing because she's too fired up to self-censor — implying the document is going to be profanity-laden civic legislation.
jokes.explanation: 1,000 Red Bulls is a good Leslie hyperbole, but the payoff — pre-warning Ben about the draft's profanity level — is the sharper joke. Leslie writing a swear-filled policy document is a funny visual.

jokes.text: Congressman Murray: 'Hey, be careful out there. Traffic is nuts on the streets and roads.' April: 'No! They got you!'
jokes.setup: The congressman is seeing Ben and April off.
jokes.punchline: The congressman's farewell is another content-free platitude ('traffic is nuts on the streets and roads' — where else would traffic be?), and April's 'No! They got you!' implies that even April, who wanted to assassinate him, is sad about his intellectual vacancy.
jokes.explanation: The running gag pays off beautifully. 'Traffic is nuts on the streets and roads' is the dumbest possible thing to say — the tautological 'streets and roads' is perfect — and April's 'No! They got you!' is a surprisingly emotional reaction from the show's most nihilistic character. The line implies April had hoped the congressman was somehow above this, and his banality has finally broken through her armor.

jokes.text: Tom arrives in DC: 'Yo, you ready to go?' April, immediately: 'Why, yes, I am, April!' — using April's actual name and mirroring the Murray introduction joke.
jokes.setup: Tom and April are heading out somewhere together in DC.
jokes.punchline: April answers for herself using her own name ('I am, April') — a slight non-sequitur that may be a character quirk joke or mild absurdism.
jokes.explanation: The transcript reads slightly ambiguously here — April's 'Why, yes I am, April!' seems to be her answering for herself using her own name, which is mildly funny as absurdism but doesn't land as cleanly as other April jokes. Weakest of the April bits.

jokes.text: Tom stares at Murray: 'No! They got you!' — as if Murray has become a screen.
jokes.setup: Murray says 'wonderful' and delivers robotic pleasantries.
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'No! They got you!' — treating Murray's hollow enthusiasm as if it's the same addictive emptiness as screens — merges the episode's two plotlines.
jokes.explanation: A smart structural joke that connects the Tom screen addiction plot with the Murray robot plot. Tom sees Murray's robotic pleasantness as another addictive empty content experience. The merging of two episode themes in one reaction is elegant writing.

jokes.text: The congressman runs into Ben and April and says 'Terrific! Hey, I'm hungry. Let's go eat some batteries... I mean, human food.' April also plays along: 'Hey, batteries... I mean, human food sounds good to me.'
jokes.setup: The robot joke has been running all episode. April's 'No! They got you!' just established that the congressman is definitely using hollow language.
jokes.punchline: The congressman accidentally says 'batteries' before correcting to 'human food,' and April immediately mirrors the slip — confirming for the audience that there is something deeply wrong with this man (and/or April is messing with him).
jokes.explanation: The perfect ending to the congressman running gag. The show commits fully — he actually says 'batteries' instead of 'food.' April's immediate, deadpan mirroring ('batteries... I mean, human food sounds good to me') is genius: it's unclear if April is trolling him or if she's also a robot, or if she's just decided to commit to the bit for her own amusement. Ben's completely overwhelmed reaction sells it. This is a well-constructed running gag payoff that justifies 8.0 craft.

tmdb_overview: An STD outbreak amongst Pawnee seniors prompts Leslie to conduct a sex education class. Meanwhile, Ron helps Tom adjust to life without technology after his gadgets are taken away, and Ben and April meet Congressman Murray for the first time.
insight: Sex education topic generates 70 jokes in 36 minutes, but 76 score suggests uneven landing.
